neutral_facts.value: The accused, who was the proprietor of a chain of hotels, abducted the victim and his wife, then later murdered the victim to marry the wife. The victim's wife provided detailed testimony about the accused's intentions and actions, including the abduction and subsequent murder. The accused were identified through circumstantial evidence, including the recovery of personal belongings and the identification of the victim's body. The accused were also linked through hotel records and the recovery of a wallet containing the victim's photograph. The prosecution's case was supported by the testimony of multiple witnesses, including the victim's wife and her mother, as well as the identification of the body through various methods, including superimposition tests. The accused were found to have taken the victim away in a car and murdered him, then disposed of the body in a forest area.

quotes.text: The judgment of the Court was delivered by MOHAN M. SHANTANAGOUDAR, J. 1. The judgment dated 19.03.2009 passed in Criminal Appeal No. 637 and 748 of 2004 passed by the High Court of Judicature at Madras whereby the High Court convicted the accused appellants for the abduction and murder of one Santhakumar, husband of the complainant Jeevajothi (PW1), is called into question in these appeals.

prosecution_argument.value: The prosecution argued that the accused no.1 wanted to take PW1 as his third wife, knowing she was already married to the deceased, and made several attempts to sever the relationship between PW1 and her husband. The murder of the deceased was committed to marry PW1 without obstruction. The evidence of PW1 and PW2, along with the recovery of the deceased's belongings and identification of the body, supported the prosecution's case.

defence_argument.value: The defence argued that the murder was a continuation of the earlier abduction incident and that the two events were part of the same investigation. They also challenged the reliability of the identification of the body through superimposition and DNA evidence, asserting that the absence of DNA testing made the identification improper.

legal_principle_applied.value: The Supreme Court applied the principle that circumstantial evidence, when conclusive and consistent, can establish guilt. It also emphasized that opinion evidence, including DNA and superimposition tests, is advisory and not binding on the court.
